title: What the Kremlin Really Thinks About Americans
hook: They don't hate you. Hate would mean you matter as a person. In the file they keep on you, you are weather. A climate that repeats. And weather, they have learned, is something you wait out.

levels.name: The Cartoon
beats: The first American they ever meet is not a person. It is a commercial. White teeth. A red cup the size of a head. A family that hugs in a kitchen so bright it looks like a film set, because it is.
You are taught to them as volume. You talk in restaurants like the room is empty. You ask a stranger what they do for a living before you ask their name. You wear logos on purpose.

In the classroom they draw you with a flag on the sleeve and no idea where Kaliningrad is. That drawing is not an insult. It is an operating assumption. A man who cannot find you on a map will not find your pressure points either. Until he does.

They log the smile. Americans smile at service workers, at cameras, at people who have not earned it. In their notes, a smile is not kindness. It is a tell. It means you want to be liked more than you want to win.

They watch your movies the way a surgeon watches an X-ray. The hero who breaks the rules and is rewarded. The president who is secretly good. The war that ends in a speech. They do not believe the movies. They believe that you do.

By the time a real American walks into a real room, the cartoon is already sitting in the other chair. You will spend the first twenty minutes fighting a drawing of yourself. Most of you never notice.

levels.name: The Customer
beats: The second file is thinner and more expensive. It is the file on what you buy. Not what you say. What you buy.

You will sell a principle for a cheaper flight. You will sell a friendship for a better rate. You will sell a secret, they are certain, for a feeling: being the smartest man at a table of people who already know.

Money is the lazy recruiter's tool. They do not lead with money. They lead with access. A conference in Vienna. A think-tank panel. A private dinner where someone important remembered your paper. Ego is cheaper than cash and it does not show up on a bank statement.

They have a joke about this that does not translate well. It is about a man who cannot be bought, and how long it takes to find the thing he will trade himself for. In the joke, it is never money. In the joke, it is always being taken seriously.

You think of yourself as a citizen. They think of you as a market. Markets have seasons. Markets punish hesitation. Markets, above all, come back after they crash and ask for the same product with a new slogan.
That is the most useful sentence in the whole file. You come back.

levels.name: The Soldier Who Won't Come
beats: They respect the hardware. They will tell you that in private, and they are not lying. Carriers. Satellites. A budget that looks like a hallucination when you write it in rubles.
They do not respect the will. That is the split, and everything after it hangs on that split.

They counted the years in Afghanistan. They counted the years in Iraq. They counted how long a democracy argues with itself before the arguing becomes the mission. They have a number for that, and they have tested it.
You will bomb a mountain. You will not occupy a winter. You will send a speech to a city you will not walk through. You will announce a red line and then hold a hearing about the announcement.
Their planners do not need you to be weak. They need you to be busy. A superpower with three crises and a midterm is, to them, a superpower with no crises at all.

The soldier in the file is not a coward. He is a man whose country will bring him home the moment the pictures get bad. They plan around the pictures. They plan around your evening news. They plan around the fact that you have one.

levels.name: The Four-Year Man
beats: This is the page they underline. You replace the entire foreign policy of a nuclear state the way other countries replace a cabinet minister. On a Tuesday. With a parade.
A treaty is not a treaty. It is a mood. A mood that expires in January. They have watched you sign, unsign, resign, and then hold a press conference about values.

They do not take your word. They take your calendar. How many months until your election. How many months until the other party's primary. How many months until the man who shook their hand is explaining himself to a committee.

You think consistency is a virtue. They think consistency is a vulnerability they do not have to worry about in you. A country that cannot keep a promise for eight years cannot keep a coalition for eight years either.

The useful move, in their doctrine, is not to convince you. It is to wait until you convince yourselves of the opposite of whatever you said last year. You are very good at that. You call it a mandate.

Somewhere in a building with bad heating, a man draws a line through a name and writes a date next to it. The date is Inauguration Day. The name is whoever you just elected. The file does not change. Only the heading does.

levels.name: The Choir
beats: They do not need to invent your arguments. You publish them. You fund them. You put them on the internet with a donate button.

A university panel about your own decline. A journalist who hates the Pentagon more than he hates their tanks. A celebrity who will read a statement about a war they could not find on a map an hour ago. The choir is not secret. The choir has a mailing list.
In the old building they used to plant stories. Now they retweet. The skill is the same. Find the American who is already angry at America and give him a bigger room.
You call this a marketplace of ideas. They call it a buffet. They do not have to be the chef. They only have to be hungry at the right hour.

The most valuable American in the file is not a spy. It is a sincere person. Sincere people do not need to be recruited. They need to be amplified. They will do the rest on their own time, in their own voice, at no cost to the budget.
If you are waiting for a villain in a dark coat to hand someone an envelope, you have misunderstood the century. The envelope is a quote. The quote is yours.

levels.name: The Neighbor in London
beats: The Americans they actually drink with are not the cartoon. They are the ones in Mayfair. In Geneva. On a yacht that is registered nowhere and docked everywhere.

These Americans speak quietly. They know where the money sits when it is tired of flags. They will lecture a camera about democracy at lunch and ask, at dinner, whether the sanction list has a loophole with a name on it.

This is the file's most dangerous page, because it is the most intimate. It is the page that says you are not a people. You are two countries sharing a language. One of them votes. One of them invoices.

They have watched a senator's son sit at a table his father could not be seen at. They have watched a foundation pay for a conversation that a ministry could not. They do not moralize about it. Moralizing is your hobby.
In their private language, this American is not a hypocrite. Hypocrisy would require a standard. This American is a professional. Professionals can be scheduled.
The cartoon still exists. It is for television. The neighbor in London is for the work. You would not recognize which one you are. That is the point of the drawing.

levels.name: The Machine
beats: They have a cleaner word for your politics than you do. They call it a machine. Machines have tolerances. Machines jam. Machines, if you study them long enough, make the same noise before they fail.
Fifty percent plus one. That is the whole religion. Not truth. Not competence. Fifty percent plus one, and then four years of the winner pretending the loser was never real.
They do not need to pick your president. They need to pick your argument. An argument that lasts from August to November is, to them, a strategic pause they did not have to pay for.

You think they want you divided. That is too flattering. Division is a side effect. What they want is your attention spent inward, on each other, on a clip, on a hearing, on a man in a supermarket who said the wrong thing into a phone.
A country staring at itself cannot stare at a border. They have measured this. They will keep measuring it. Every time your news cycle eats a week, someone else's map gets a new road.
The machine is not evil in the file. Evil is a movie word. The machine is predictable. Predictable is the highest compliment their planners give to an enemy.

levels.name: The Next One
beats: A new American walks onto a stage and talks about reset. About strength. About a line that will not be crossed this time. The room with the bad heating does not cheer and does not panic. Someone opens the same folder.

The cartoon is still in it. The customer. The soldier who will not stay. The four-year man. The choir. The neighbor. The machine. The headings have not moved in thirty years. Only the photographs have.
They do not need you to be worse. They need you to be you: loud, rich, impatient, convinced that history is a sequel in which you still have the best effects budget.

You will ask, at the end of a video like this, whether they are right. That question is also in the file. Americans love a verdict. They love to put themselves on the scale and argue with the reading.
The file does not care about the verdict. The file cares that you watched, that you felt seen or insulted, and that tomorrow you will argue about it with each other instead of looking up.

Someone new is already writing a speech about how this time will be different. In the building with the bad heating, they sharpen a pencil. The cycle does not continue because they are brilliant. It continues because you are familiar.
